es: Escribir un relato propio de 240–300 palabras con escena mostrada, ritmo controlado, giro preparado, desenlace que cierra la pregunta inicial y un toque de humor o ironía.

vocabulary.es: preparar la escena, situar al lector

teaching.en: A story should set the scene with vivid detail instead of a summary: rain tapped the window while Tom counted his keys.
teaching.es: Un relato debe situar la escena con un detalle vívido en lugar de un resumen: la lluvia golpeaba la ventana mientras Tom contaba sus llaves.
teaching.explanationEs: Mostrar la escena con detalles concretos engancha más que contar «Tom estaba nervioso».
segments: A story should set the scene with vivid detail instead of
a summary: rain tapped the window while Tom counted his keys.
teaching.audioText: A story should set the scene with vivid detail instead of a summary: rain tapped the window while Tom counted his keys.

teaching.en: To pick up the pace, use fronting and fragments: Down the hill ran the dog. Silence.
teaching.es: Para acelerar el ritmo, usa la anteposición y los fragmentos: Colina abajo corrió el perro. Silencio.
teaching.explanationEs: Con anteposición, el lugar va primero y el sujeto sigue al verbo; las frases sin verbo aceleran el relato.
segments: To pick up the pace, use fronting and
fragments: Down the hill ran the dog. Silence.
teaching.audioText: To pick up the pace, use fronting and fragments: Down the hill ran the dog. Silence.

teaching.en: Good writers foreshadow the plot twist with a small detail early on, so that the surprise feels fair rather than cheap.
teaching.es: Quien escribe bien anticipa el giro con un pequeño detalle desde el principio, para que la sorpresa parezca justa y no barata.
teaching.explanationEs: Un giro que llega de la nada decepciona; uno sembrado con una pista se disfruta dos veces.
segments: Good writers foreshadow the plot twist with a small detail early
on, so that the surprise feels fair rather than cheap.
teaching.audioText: Good writers foreshadow the plot twist with a small detail early on, so that the surprise feels fair rather than cheap.

teaching.en: Concrete details reveal feelings better than labels: his hands shook as he folded the map, so nervous is never needed.
teaching.es: Los detalles concretos revelan los sentimientos mejor que las etiquetas: le temblaban las manos al doblar el mapa, así que nunca hace falta «nervioso».
teaching.explanationEs: Mostrar la emoción con una acción (shook) evita nombrarla: es la regla «show, don't tell».
segments: Concrete details reveal feelings better than labels: his hands shook
as he folded the map, so nervous is never needed.
teaching.audioText: Concrete details reveal feelings better than labels: his hands shook as he folded the map, so nervous is never needed.

teaching.en: A satisfying ending should tie up loose ends and reveal the answer to the question raised at the start.
teaching.es: Un desenlace satisfactorio debe atar los cabos sueltos y revelar la respuesta a la pregunta planteada al principio.
teaching.explanationEs: El final cierra el círculo: lo que se preguntaba al empezar recibe respuesta, aunque sea con un encogimiento de hombros.
segments: A satisfying ending should tie up loose ends and reveal
the answer to the question raised at the start.
teaching.audioText: A satisfying ending should tie up loose ends and reveal the answer to the question raised at the start.

teaching.en: A touch of irony, delivered deadpan, is enough: the taxi, of course, arrived after the wedding, and nobody mentioned it.
teaching.es: Basta un toque de ironía, dicho con cara seria: el taxi, por supuesto, llegó después de la boda y nadie lo mencionó.
teaching.explanationEs: Of course dicho de algo que ocurre al revés de lo esperado es ironía amable; el tono impasible la hace más graciosa.
segments: A touch of irony, delivered deadpan, is enough: the taxi,
of course, arrived after the wedding, and nobody mentioned it.
teaching.audioText: A touch of irony, delivered deadpan, is enough: the taxi, of course, arrived after the wedding, and nobody mentioned it.

prompt.es: ¿Qué frase muestra el nerviosismo sin nombrarlo?

choices.text: She was extremely nervous about the map and the long meeting.
Her hands shook as she folded the map, and twice she dropped the pen.
She felt very nervous while she looked at the map and the clock.

feedback.es: Una acción concreta (las manos que tiemblan, el bolígrafo que cae) deja ver el nervio; las otras frases solo lo etiquetan.

hint.es: Busca el detalle físico, no la etiqueta de la emoción.

prompt.es: Ordena con anteposición: «En la habitación entró un desconocido.»

answer.text: Into the room walked a stranger

feedback.es: Con anteposición, el lugar va primero y el sujeto sigue al verbo: Into the room walked a stranger.

hint.es: Empieza por el lugar; el sujeto va detrás del verbo.

prompt.es: Completa: «Una pista sembrada en la primera escena lo anticipa y hace justa la sorpresa.»

feedback.es: Foreshadow es el verbo de sembrar una pista que anticipa un giro posterior, para que no parezca arbitrario.

hint.es: Verbo que significa anticipar algo con una pista previa.

origin.text: The plot twist should be prepared early. A small clue, planted in the first scene, will ___ it, so that the surprise feels fair.

prompt.es: ¿Qué efecto logra el final de este fragmento?

choices.text: It proves that Mia was right to avoid her neighbour all week.
It shows that the neighbour is hiding a serious secret.
It introduces a new character who will solve the problem.
It turns a frightening idea into a small, funny reveal.

feedback.es: Mia temía una conversación grave y el vecino solo quería avisarle de una luz encendida: el contraste produce el giro cómico.

origin.text: For a week Mia avoided the lift because the neighbour from upstairs kept trying to talk to her. On Friday, cornered at last, she listened to him for ten minutes. He only wanted to tell her that her bicycle lights had been on since Monday.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige cómo trata el narrador el aviso de la empresa.

choices.text: He praises with a straight face what he really finds silly.
He sincerely thanks the company for thinking of its customers.
He complains in anger that nobody answers the phone.

feedback.es: El narrador alaba con cara seria algo absurdo (cerrar el único día de visita): es ironía impasible, no agradecimiento sincero.

origin.audio: The company sent an email announcing that, for the convenience of customers, the office would be closed on the only day customers could visit. The narrator thanked them warmly for thinking of everybody, and added that the silence on the phone line had been particularly moving.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase del relato con su función.

pairs: Rain tapped on the roof while Leo counted coins
Out of the fog stepped a man in a yellow coat
The key had been in her pocket all along
In the end, nobody mentioned the cake
How kind of the airline to lose my suitcase

feedback.es: Cada frase cumple una función distinta: mostrar, acelerar, sorprender, cerrar y ironizar.

prompt.es: Escucha el taller y elige qué opina la tutora del final del alumno.

choices.text: It is too short to answer the question raised at the start.
It spoils the good work of the opening by explaining too much.
It moves the attention from the man to the other passengers.
It would work better with a stronger plot twist.

feedback.es: La tutora elogia el comienzo, que muestra la soledad sin nombrarla, pero critica que el final la explique: quien recibe el significado deja de buscarlo.

origin.audio: In this week's writing workshop, the tutor read out a student's opening. Rain tapped the window of a night bus, a man counted his coins twice, and nobody looked up from their phones. She stopped there and said that the student had not written the word lonely once, yet every reader had felt it. She added, however, that the ending spoiled everything: the bus stopped, the man stepped off, and the writer explained in three sentences what the story had meant. A reader who is told the meaning, she said, stops looking for it.

prompt.es: ¿Qué le recomienda realmente Ana a Leo en su mensaje?

choices.text: To explain the glasses joke earlier, so that nobody misses it.
To soften the deadpan tone with a warmer, more personal narrator.
To trust the reader and stop before the joke is explained.
To keep the ending but shorten the kitchen scene.

feedback.es: Ana elogia la escena y el giro, pero sugiere cortar las dos últimas frases: que el lector disfrute el silencio sin que se le explique el chiste.

origin.text: Hi Leo, I read your draft on the train. The scene in the kitchen is vivid, and the twist about the glasses made me laugh. My only doubt is the ending: you explain the joke after telling it, and deadpan works best when the narrator keeps a straight face. If I were you, I would cut the last two sentences and let the reader enjoy the silence.

prompt.es: Completa: «Un buen inicio prepara la escena con un detalle vívido: una radio, un abrigo.»

feedback.es: Set the scene es la colocación para situar al lector con un detalle concreto en lugar de un resumen.

origin.text: A strong opening does not give a summary of the evening. Instead, it tries to ___ the scene with one vivid detail: a radio playing, a half-eaten sandwich, a coat left on the floor.

prompt.es: Escribe tu relato (180–300 palabras): escena, ritmo, giro, final e ironía.

answer.text: Rain tapped the window of the night bus. Tom counted his coins twice, and then a third time, while his foot beat the floor. Behind him, a man in a grey suit sighed at his own watch. On Tom's knees lay the folder with his drawings, and his hands would not stay still. The driver hummed a cheerful song, which made everything worse. Off the bus he jumped, and up the stairs he ran. Silence in the corridor. A closed door. He was sure he had missed the interview by ten minutes, and he had practised his speech all week. Then a woman appeared at the end of the hall, holding a cup of tea. "Are you Tom?" she asked. "We had to postpone everything. The director, of course, is stuck in traffic." Tom laughed so loudly that the secretary looked up. It turned out that the director had been sitting behind him on the bus all along, and he arrived five minutes later, out of breath, blaming the driver's song. In the end, Tom got the job, and the driver got a thank-you card.
accepted: Rain tapped the window of the night bus. Tom counted his coins twice, and then a third time, while his foot beat the floor. Behind him, a man in a grey suit sighed at his own watch. On Tom's knees lay the folder with his drawings, and his hands would not stay still. The driver hummed a cheerful song, which made everything worse. Off the bus he jumped, and up the stairs he ran. Silence in the corridor. A closed door. He was sure he had missed the interview by ten minutes, and he had practised his speech all week. Then a woman appeared at the end of the hall, holding a cup of tea. "Are you Tom?" she asked. "We had to postpone everything. The director, of course, is stuck in traffic." Tom laughed so loudly that the secretary looked up. It turned out that the director had been sitting behind him on the bus all along, and he arrived five minutes later, out of breath, blaming the driver's song. In the end, Tom got the job, and the driver got a thank-you card.

Every Sunday my grandfather fished at the lake, and every Sunday he came home with an empty bucket and a happy face. My mother laughed and said that fishing was only an excuse to sit in silence. One morning I followed him. Into the water went his line, and out of the silence came nothing. Hours passed. Nobody spoke, and even the gulls seemed to be waiting for something to happen. The lake stayed as still as a painting. Then a tiny silver fish jumped into the bucket by itself. My grandfather stared at it. His hands shook a little as he lifted the bucket. I had never seen him so excited, or so suspicious. "Of course," he said at last, "the day I bring a friend, the fish behave." It turned out that he had been hiding a secret all along: he had never caught a single fish, and he was delighted about it. In the end, he let the fish go and told everybody it was the best catch of his life. Since then, he has never fished alone.

feedback.es: Un relato completo muestra la escena, controla el ritmo, prepara un giro, cierra con un desenlace y suma una ironía amable.

origin.text: Cuenta una historia corta con: una escena mostrada con detalles concretos, una anteposición o fragmentos, un giro sembrado con una pista, un desenlace y un toque de humor o ironía.

prompt.es: Convierte «Mia was furious.» en una frase que muestre la ira sin nombrarla.

answer.text: Mia slammed the door so hard that the glasses rattled on the shelf.
accepted: Mia slammed the door so hard that the glasses rattled on the shelf.
Mia clenched her fists as she stared at the closed door.
Mia gripped her pen until her knuckles turned white.

feedback.es: Mostrar es sustituir la etiqueta (furious) por un gesto observable y sus consecuencias: un portazo, unos puños apretados.

prompt.es: ¿Qué tono adopta el narrador ante la puntualidad del fontanero?

choices.text: Admiring: he is the only worker who kept his promise.
Sorry for him: the delay was caused by other people.
Neutral: the narrator simply reports the order of events.
Ironic: the praise hides that he arrived far too late.

feedback.es: El narrador celebra la puntualidad de un fontanero que llegó dos horas después de que empezara la inundación: la alabanza dice lo contrario de lo que piensa, y eso es ironía.

origin.text: The plumber arrived at four, exactly as promised, and put his tools down in the kitchen. Mia was delighted. Tom, who had been waiting since noon, thanked him for being on time. The flood, as it happened, had started at two, and the neighbours were already carrying their bags down the stairs.

prompt.es: Ordena con anteposición: «En el jardín entró un hombre con abrigo amarillo.»

answer.text: Into the garden walked a man in a yellow coat

feedback.es: Con anteposición, el lugar va primero y el sujeto sigue al verbo: Into the garden walked a man.
